article.title: Sanctuary: Borders & Belonging in 2026
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: by Bleu Cease, Curator Rochester Contemporary Art Center (RoCo) presents Sanctuary: Borders & Belonging in 2026 , an exhibition bringing together national and regional artists, creatives, and documentarians in response to the current political and social landscape surrounding immigration. On view October 2 through November 14, 2026, the exhibition centers the human lives behind political rhetoric, examining how belonging is made and denied, and how care, resilience, and solidarity persist amid increasingly hostile systems and cruel public narratives. * * * Sanctuary is on view through November 14. Sanctuary: Borders & Belonging in 2026 brings together national and regional artists, creatives, documentarians, and community members in response to the political and social realities surrounding immigration and migration. The exhibition amplifies immigrant voices, documents criminalization and detention, examines border politics and architecture, and creates space for people to share the complex experiences that shape belonging. Through testimony and creative resistance, these projects center the human lives behind political rhetoric while also countering simplistic and divisive narratives, insisting on dignity and human rights for all. Together, they ask how belonging is made and denied, and how care, solidarity, and resilience persist in the face The installation honoring Dolores Bustamante, created in collaboration with Erica Bryant and Carly Fox, places portraits of a generous farmworker, grandmother, and community leader alongside 137 letters of support, turning a local campaign for her release into a public shrine honoring the woman at the center and our community’s mutual aid, collective care, and resistance to immigrant detention. Bringing Tom Policano’s photographs from Slim Pickins into conversation with Cher Valentino’s recent paintings inspired by those images, this installation connects the conditions of migrant farmworkers documented in the 1970s to their continued vulnerability today. The pairing reminds us that poverty and unjust labor practices persist, now compounded by immigration enforcement targeting these workers, compressing decades of limited progress into an urgent shared present. Julio Salgado’s project I Am UndocuQueer features heavily alongside the artist’s own personal reflections in the video My Name Is Julio , making visible undocumented queer people’s leading role in the immigrant-rights movement, and confronting fear with pride, humor, joy, and self-representation, even in the face of deportation. Arleene Correa Valencia’s textile artworks transform family photographs, letters, clothing, and culturally specific fabrics into haunting portraits of migration, family separation, memory, and longing; where incomplete or absent figures represent the lives interrupted by borders, policies, and immigration enforcement. The exhibition premiers Sound of Sanctuary , a ten-track album, installed as a listening station in the gallery. Sound of Sanctuary , an immersive listening installation, created by Anaglog (Sean Mulligan) in partnership with RoCo, launches a live-recorded album and brings together five first- and second-generation immigrant artists and five Rochester musicians with the understanding that sanctuary is not a fixed place, but a shared culture of listening, relationship, attention, and care The Community Interview Project: The Immigrant Experience presents nearly 100 intimate recordings with immigrants from Rochester and the surrounding region into the gallery, grounding political debates in the voices and stories of our neighbors, presenting immigration as a diverse collection of lived experiences through which this community and the U.S. as a country have continually been built. (I’m)Migration is an exhibition within an exhibition; a collection resulting from an open call for visual art by immigrants in the Rochester region. It includes more than 60 artworks by immigrants and immigrant collaborators, bringing together stories of arrival, belonging, separation, resilience, cultural practice, and transformation while emphasizing the power of many voices speaking alongside one another. The short advocacy film When They Come For Me: Hope and Fear for Immigrants in the Promised Land by Worldwide Documentaries brings together local immigrant advocates and community perspectives to document the effects of inhumane immigration policies in Rochester, the Finger Lakes region, and Western New York. In Border Wall and several accompanying photographs, Saman and Sasan Oskouei use mirrors, fencing, barbed wire, and steel to fracture the apparent permanence of borders, transforming barriers into boats, doorways, flowers, flags, and passages toward freedom, movement, and envisioning another future. Jim Mott’s ICE Detention Facilities and the American Landscape (Seven Studies) uses paintings based on field observation and digital reconnaissance to consider how the growing for-profit immigration detention system has become embedded within familiar rural and urban communities, connecting the concrete realities of incarceration to the economic decline, infrastructure, and broader culture of the places that host and enable it. Saints of Our Time by Pamela Araya In Resist or Surrender , Annette Dragon’s compassionate photographs show that resistance is not an exceptional act but an ongoing local practice. She honors the ordinary people who gather throughout the region to advocate for immigrants and human rights while holding close the personal absence of her friend who is imprisoned at a nearby detention center. Saints of Our Time by Pamela Araya reimagines Catholic devotional portraiture through three highly visible contemporary figures connected to immigration, Latin American identity, and cultural memory. The three paintings honor Liam Conejo Ramos in Hope , Bad Bunny in Voice , and Renée Good in Testimony , as embodiments of suffering, cultural power, courage, and the ongoing struggle for dignity and belonging. Pamela Dodds’s installation Documenting Border Barriers transforms meticulously rendered drypoint etchings of fences, walls, razor wire, and surveillance systems into an imposing visual and information archive of the architecture of exclusion. It arranges the prints like a wall across the gallery and reveals these structures as deliberate, mostly contemporary acts of political control. Pamela Dodds’s Documenting Border Barriers considers the physical structures that divide nations and restrict movement. Installed outside the gallery, the related work of public art BELONG by Gianna Stewart confronts censorship and erasure by incorporating hundreds of words that have been removed from government websites, publications, and grant applications into a large graphic. This brave artwork makes visible the absurdity and the danger of this attempted erasure, while also reclaiming public space to insist that we all belong. Sanctuary: Borders & Belonging in 2026 continues RoCo’s longstanding support for artists who engage urgent social and political questions. It also reaffirms our commitment to art practices that center testimony, witnessing, imagination, and action. At a time of censorship and fear, the exhibition amplifies artists who, often at great personal or professional risk, speak truth to power and advocate for human rights and a more just, equitable world. As global inequality, climate change, and the politics of fear lead to increasingly barricaded and surveilled borders, and immigrant communities face intensified criminalization, Sanctuary demands solidarity. To listen to one another. To defend one another. And to recognize that our freedom and safety are bound together. Upcoming Events: Film Screening: Ice Breaker / Match Maker . [ Friday, October 16, 6:00pm – 9:00pm] A screening and related gathering exploring migration, connection, and the social realities of immigrant life. Surviving Suppression: How Artists Experience and Overcome Censorship. [Friday, October 23, 2026, 6:30pm – 9:00pm] A panel and conversation examining the pressures artists face when their work addresses politically charged subjects, and the strategies they use to continue speaking through art. Sound of Sanctuary: LIVE . [Friday, November 13, 6:30pm ] A live performance of Sound of Sanctuary which is being launched in partnership with RoCo as an installation and listening station in the main gallery. Sanctuary: Borders & Belonging in 2026 will be on view October 2 – November 14, 2026, at Rochester Contemporary Art Center, [ 137 East Avenue ]. Gallery hours are Wednesday – Sunday, 12:00pm – 5:00pm, with extended hours Fridays until 9:00pm. Suggested admission is $2; admission is free for RoCo members.
